title: Keeping Your Brain Healthy
hook: No pill prevents dementia, but the habits that protect your heart turn out to protect your brain too.
key_points: Physical activity is among the best-supported habits for brain health.
Managing blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol protects the brain.
Staying socially and mentally engaged is linked to better cognitive health.
Good sleep and not smoking support long-term brain function.
Evidence points to lower risk, not a guarantee; no supplement is proven to prevent dementia.
content_html: There's no magic pill that prevents dementia, and the National Institute on Aging is candid about that. What the evidence does support is encouraging: many of the same habits that keep your heart healthy also appear to protect your brain as you age.
extra_html:
According to the NIA, regular physical activity is among the best-supported habits for cognitive health. Controlling blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol matters too, since the brain depends on healthy blood vessels. Staying socially connected and mentally engaged, getting good sleep, eating well, and not smoking round out the picture.

It's worth being precise about what this means. These habits are linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline, not a guarantee against it, and the NIA notes that no dietary supplement has been proven to prevent dementia. The practical takeaway is reassuringly ordinary: the moves that are good for the rest of you are also your best bet for your brain.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

related.title: Understanding Blood Pressure
related.hook: High blood pressure is called the 'silent killer' for a reason — it usually has no symptoms, yet it quietly raises your risk of heart attack and stroke.

related.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes
related.hook: Type 2 diabetes often arrives slowly, with a warning stage called prediabetes — and at that stage, modest lifestyle changes can stop or delay it.

related.title: Why Sleep Matters
related.hook: Sleep isn't downtime — it's when your brain consolidates memory and your body repairs itself. Skimp on it for long and the bill comes due in your health.

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

related.title: Your Brain Can Keep Improving — Even in Your 90s
related.hook: A three-year study of nearly 4,000 adults aged 19 to 94 found brain health can improve at any age, challenging the assumption that mental sharpness only declines with the years.

related.title: The Link Between Diabetes and Dementia
related.hook: Diabetes and dementia keep turning up together — and it may be no coincidence. Trouble with insulin and blood sugar can starve, inflame, and damage the brain's blood vessels.

flashcards.prompt: What's the honest summary of how lifestyle relates to brain health?
flashcards.back_html: Healthy habits like exercise, managing blood pressure and blood sugar, staying socially engaged, sleeping well, and not smoking are linked to lower risk of cognitive decline. They tilt the odds, but no habit or supplement is proven to prevent dementia.

flashcards.prompt: Which is best supported by evidence for protecting cognitive health?

choices.text: Avoiding all mental challenges to rest the brain

flashcards.explanation_html: Physical activity is among the most strongly supported habits for brain health. No supplement is proven to prevent dementia, and staying mentally engaged helps rather than hurts.
